title: Eclampsia: management of a fit
prompt: A 22-year-old at 37 weeks has just had a generalised fit on the ward; BP 170/115 mmHg.
steps: Call for help, note the time and do not leave her alone; protect her from injury, do not restrain her and put nothing in her mouth.
After the fit place her in the left lateral position, clear and suction the airway and give oxygen 4-6 L/min by mask.
Get IV access (16-18 G) and draw bloods: FBC, LFT, creatinine, clotting, glucose, malaria test and group and cross-match.
Give the MgSO4 loading dose immediately (Pritchard: 4 g IV plus 10 g IM, 5 g in each buttock).
Check blood glucose and the malaria test and treat what you find; treat BP of 160/110 or more (nifedipine 10 mg orally if she can swallow safely, otherwise hydralazine 5 mg IV).
Catheterise with strict input and output charting, restrict fluids to about 80 mL/h, and assess the fetus (bradycardia usually recovers in 3-5 minutes; resuscitate the mother first).
Deliver within 12 hours of the fit once she is stable, and continue MgSO4 for 24 hours after delivery or the last fit.
why: Protect the airway and give MgSO4 before anything else; the fetal bradycardia after a fit settles once the mother is oxygenated, so resuscitate her before rushing to theatre.

title: Primary PPH: the E-MOTIVE bundle
prompt: A woman delivered 10 minutes ago; the calibrated drape shows 700 mL and bleeding continues.
steps: Call for help and note the time; lay her flat, give oxygen, and put in two large-bore IV cannulae and take bloods including a clotting test.
M: massage the uterine fundus firmly until it is hard, expelling clots.
O: give oxytocin 10 IU IV slowly (or IM), then start an oxytocin infusion.
T: give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes (within 3 hours of birth), repeating after 30 minutes if bleeding continues.
I: give a warmed crystalloid bolus of 500 mL to 1 L, reassess, and start blood as soon as it is available.
Empty the bladder with a Foley catheter, then examine the genital tract: is the placenta complete, and are there tears, a haematoma or an inversion?
E: escalate if bleeding continues despite the bundle (second-line drugs, bimanual compression, tamponade, theatre, early referral) and monitor every 15 minutes.
why: The bundle is started together and early, driven by objective measurement with the calibrated drape, rather than one drug at a time while waiting to see what works.

title: Shoulder dystocia: HELPERR
prompt: The head has delivered and then retracts against the perineum (turtle sign) in a woman with a 4.4 kg baby.
steps: H: call for help (midwife, obstetrician, paediatrician, anaesthetist), stop her pushing and note the time the head was delivered.
E: evaluate for an episiotomy to make room for internal manoeuvres (it does not free the shoulder on its own).
L: McRoberts manoeuvre, hyperflexing both thighs onto the abdomen.
P: suprapubic pressure by an assistant on the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder (never fundal pressure).
E: enter the vagina for internal rotation manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw).
R: remove the posterior arm by following it to the elbow, flexing it and sweeping it across the chest.
R: roll her onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre) and retry the manoeuvres.
why: McRoberts and suprapubic pressure resolve most cases, so they come before internal manoeuvres; never pull hard on the head (Erb's palsy) or push on the fundus (worsens impaction).

title: Umbilical cord prolapse
prompt: After artificial rupture of membranes at 38 weeks, a pulsating loop of cord is felt in the vagina and the fetal heart is slow.
steps: Call for help, note the time and stop any oxytocin.
Do not handle the cord (it causes vasospasm); if it is outside the vagina, replace it gently or cover it with warm saline-soaked gauze.
Relieve compression by pushing the presenting part up with fingers in the vagina, or use the knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position, especially during transfer.
If a delay is expected, insert a Foley catheter and instil 500-750 mL of 0.9% saline and clamp it (empty the bladder before the uterus is opened).
If there is a delay and the CTG is abnormal, give terbutaline 0.25 mg SC as tocolysis.
Deliver by category 1 caesarean (aim for within 30 minutes), or by quick assisted vaginal birth if fully dilated; vaginal delivery if the fetus is dead.
Have a neonatal resuscitation team ready, take paired cord gases if possible and debrief the family.
why: The aim is to keep the presenting part off the cord and deliver fast; handling the cord or leaving the part pressing on it causes fetal hypoxia.

title: Maternal collapse and cardiac arrest in late pregnancy
prompt: A woman at 34 weeks collapses on the ward and does not respond.
steps: Shout for help and call the arrest team, including the obstetrician and anaesthetist and the neonatal team.
Confirm she is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
Start chest compressions without delay, with manual left uterine displacement (or a 15-30 degree left tilt) to relieve aortocaval compression.
Open the airway and ventilate with a bag-mask and oxygen, aiming for SpO2 of 95% or more.
Look for and treat reversible causes: haemorrhage (two large-bore cannulae, fluids and blood), and magnesium toxicity (calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV slowly) if she is on MgSO4.
If there is no return of circulation by 4 minutes, prepare for a perimortem caesarean (uterus at or above the umbilicus) so the baby is delivered by 4-5 minutes, continuing CPR throughout.
why: From about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the IVC, so left uterine displacement comes with the first compressions, and emptying the uterus within 4-5 minutes improves maternal resuscitation.

title: Acute uterine inversion
prompt: A woman is in profound shock minutes after delivery; the placenta was delivered with cord traction, the fundus cannot be felt and a mass is at the introitus.
steps: Call for help immediately and note the time.
Stop oxytocin and any other uterotonic, and stop pulling on the cord.
Treat shock: lay her flat, give oxygen, put in two large-bore IV lines, take bloods and give fluids.
Replace the uterus at once with the Johnson manoeuvre: push the fundus back through the cervix with the palm, the part that came out last going in first (do not remove an attached placenta first).
If that fails, use O'Sullivan hydrostatic replacement (warm saline into the vagina with the introitus sealed), or surgical correction in theatre.
After replacement give oxytocin and hold the uterus in place until it contracts, then give antibiotics.
why: Replace it immediately, before the cervix clamps down; oxytocin is stopped until the uterus is back and given straight after replacement.

title: ETAT: ABCD triage and treatment
prompt: A sick child arrives at the outpatient department with an emergency sign.
steps: Triage at the door within 15-20 seconds, before registration; any emergency sign means straight to the resuscitation area, and shout for help.
A: open the airway (head tilt-chin lift in a child, neutral position in an infant) and clear any obstruction.
B: give oxygen, or bag-mask ventilation if not breathing or gasping.
C: if there are signs of shock, insert an IV or IO line, take blood for glucose, Hb, malaria test and cross-match, and give fluids per protocol (normal child or severe acute malnutrition).
C: if comatose or convulsing, use the recovery position, check glucose and give dextrose if low, and give an anticonvulsant if fitting.
D: if there is diarrhoea with severe dehydration, start Plan C (or the SAM protocol if malnourished).
Reassess after each step, then take the history, examine fully, investigate and give specific treatment and admit.
why: Emergency signs are treated at once in ABCD order and the child is reassessed at every letter; history, examination and tests come after the emergency has been dealt with.

title: Newborn resuscitation: Helping Babies Breathe
prompt: A term baby is born and does not cry.
steps: Note the time of birth, dry the baby thoroughly, remove the wet cloth and keep warm.
If not crying, position the head slightly extended, suction only if secretions or meconium block the airway, and stimulate by rubbing the back.
If not breathing or gasping, clamp and cut the cord and start bag-mask ventilation at 40 breaths per minute, within the first minute.
If the chest is not moving, improve ventilation: reapply the mask, reposition the head, clear the airway, open the mouth slightly and squeeze harder.
After 1 minute of effective ventilation, call for help if the baby is still not breathing well and check the heart rate (count for 6 seconds and multiply by 10).
If the heart rate is 100 or more, continue ventilation until the baby breathes, then monitor; if below 100, continue, improve ventilation and arrange advanced care.
In hospital, if the heart rate is below 60 after 30 seconds of ventilation that moves the chest, start two-thumb chest compressions at 3:1 with 100% oxygen.
why: Effective ventilation within the Golden Minute is what resuscitates the baby; suction and drugs come far behind it, and the two outcome checks are chest movement and heart rate.

title: Status epilepticus in a child
prompt: A 4-year-old is brought in convulsing continuously.
steps: Place her in the recovery position, clear and suction the airway and give oxygen.
Check the blood glucose; if below 2.5 mmol/L (or you cannot check) give 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg IV over 2-3 minutes.
Treat any seizure still going at 5 minutes: give a benzodiazepine and note the time (diazepam 0.5 mg/kg rectally, or 0.2-0.3 mg/kg slow IV, or buccal midazolam).
If still fitting 10 minutes later, give a second benzodiazepine dose (never more than two doses in total, counting any given earlier).
If still fitting after the second dose, give phenobarbital 15-20 mg/kg IV over 15-20 minutes (or phenytoin) and call the senior.
Look for the cause (fever, malaria test, neck stiffness, poisoning, trauma), treat the fever, and do a lumbar puncture only when stable.
why: Airway, oxygen and glucose come before the anticonvulsant, and a third benzodiazepine dose risks respiratory arrest so the second-line drug follows the second dose.

title: Severe dehydration: Plan C
prompt: An 18-month-old with watery diarrhoea is lethargic with sunken eyes and a very slow skin pinch (no malnutrition).
steps: Start an IV (or IO) line immediately and give ORS by mouth while the drip is being set up if she can drink.
Give Ringer's lactate 30 mL/kg as fast as possible (in 30 minutes at 12 months or older; 1 hour under 12 months), repeating it once if the radial pulse is still very weak or absent.
Then give 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours (5 hours in infants under 12 months).
Reassess every 15-30 minutes and give the drip faster if hydration is not improving.
As soon as she can drink, give ORS about 5 mL/kg/h alongside the drip, and start zinc once rehydrated.
Reclassify after 3 hours (6 hours in an infant) and choose Plan A, B or C to continue.
why: The total is 100 mL/kg of Ringer's lactate with most of it given early; never plain 5% dextrose, and in severe acute malnutrition use ReSoMal instead of Plan C.

title: Anaphylaxis in a child
prompt: An 8-year-old develops stridor, hives, wheeze and shock minutes after an IV antibiotic.
steps: Stop the suspected drug (remove the trigger) and call for help.
Give adrenaline 1:1000 IM into the anterolateral thigh immediately (0.01 mL/kg; 0.3 mL for 6-12 years).
Lie her flat with the legs raised (sit her up if breathing is the main problem).
Give oxygen, insert an IV or IO line and give crystalloid 10 mL/kg if shocked.
Repeat adrenaline every 5 minutes if not improving, and call the senior or anaesthetist after two IM doses.
Give chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone as second-line drugs only; they never replace adrenaline.
Observe for at least 6-12 hours for a biphasic reaction and document the trigger.
why: IM adrenaline is the first and life-saving drug; antihistamines and steroids are second-line and slow, so they come after it.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis: the first hours
prompt: A 10-year-old with vomiting, deep sighing breathing and drowsiness has glucose 29 mmol/L and ketonuria 3+.
steps: Assess airway and breathing (recovery position, NG tube if vomiting and drowsy), and give oxygen if SpO2 is below 94% or she is shocked.
Give 0.9% saline: 20 mL/kg rapidly if shocked, or 10-20 mL/kg over 20-60 minutes if not shocked.
Weigh her, check glucose and ketones, and record a baseline GCS; take bloods before treatment (venous gas, sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine, FBC, malaria test).
Call the senior and start the DKA flow chart with hourly observations.
Continue 0.9% saline for the deficit plus maintenance over 24-48 hours, adding potassium chloride once potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L and she is passing urine.
After 1-2 hours of fluids start soluble insulin 0.05-0.1 units/kg/h IV, with NO insulin bolus, and watch for cerebral oedema.
why: Fluids come first, insulin follows 1-2 hours later with no bolus, and correction is steady because cerebral oedema is the main cause of DKA death in children.
